## The problem

Our team of twelve maintains feature branches that routinely live for two to three weeks before merging. By the time a branch is ready, it has drifted so far from main that integration becomes its own project: merge conflicts sprawl across a dozen files, CI fails for reasons unrelated to the feature itself, and reviewers must reconstruct context for changes that no longer resemble the original diff. Last quarter, three releases slipped specifically because "merge week" uncovered integration problems no one had budgeted time for. We are paying an integration tax that compounds with every day a branch stays open, and it is landing hardest on our most productive contributors, who are also our most prolific branchers.

## The proposal

- Adopt trunk-based development: all engineers commit small, reviewed changes directly to main at least once a day, guarded by feature flags for anything not ready for users.
- Break work into vertical slices that can be merged within 24 hours, even if the full feature ships incrementally behind a flag.
- Strengthen CI so main is always releasable — fast tests on every push, a red build treated as top priority.
- Set a short-lived-branch policy: branches older than two days get flagged in standup for help unblocking them.
- Run a 30-day pilot with two squads before rolling out team-wide, so we can adjust based on real friction rather than theory.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is that trunk-based development trades a known cost (occasional painful merges) for a constant one: engineers must now discipline themselves to slice work small, write flags, and review code faster, and if any of that lapses, we risk shipping half-finished or broken logic straight to main. This is a real risk, not a hypothetical one — teams that adopt trunk-based development without investing in flagging discipline and fast CI do sometimes see more incidents, not fewer. Our mitigation is the pilot: we test the practice on two squads first, measure incident rates and cycle time, and only expand if the data supports it. We should also expect initial resistance from engineers who find comfort in an isolated branch, and slower velocity in week one as habits shift.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
